implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define (or find) one combinator that takes two or more unary functions and returns their sequential application - f then g reads left to right (pipe/andThen) or right to left (classic compose) - plus an identity function as the zero-step case. Keep every stage unary and pure; adapt multi-argument functions at the edge with partial application instead of widening the combinator. Fix one ordering convention for the whole codebase and document it next to the combinator, because the direction is the one detail every language chooses differently. When a step must fail, skip or branch, lift the chain into a container (Result/Option/stream) whose own andThen sequences it, or fall back to explicit control flow: raw composition sequences successful application only. The classic inline form (nested calls, or assignments to intermediate variables) stays justified for short one-off chains and inside performance-critical loops, where the extra call frame per step is not free.
code_sketch:
compose(f, g) = x -> g(f(x))        # classic compose, right-to-left reading
pipe(f, g)    = x -> g(f(x))        # same algebra, steps listed left-to-right
identity(x)   = x                   # zero-step chain

chain  = compose(normalize, validate, format)
result = chain(input)               # steps run in order, intermediates unnamed
pitfalls: Composition sequences successful application only: a step that returns "nothing" or an error value breaks the next step unless the chain is lifted into a Result/Option/stream abstraction.
The ordering convention is not part of the algebra: if compose and pipe both exist with different argument order, chains can be silently reversed across modules.
Erased or boxed callables (dynamic dispatch, interface wrappers, reflection) turn each step into an indirect call and can dominate the cost of the transformation itself.
Deeply nested composition (10+ steps) creates a chain of call frames that can exhaust stack space in recursive or deeply nested scenarios; split the chain or fuse critical segments.

Anonymous or point-free chains destroy diagnostic context: production stack traces and profilers show lambda frames or combinator internals instead of the failing step's name; wrap steps in named functions from the start.
Mixing right-to-left compose and left-to-right pipe/andThen helpers in one codebase silently reverses a copied chain; enforce a single ordering convention at the module or package level.

Type inference degrades along the chain: Java wildcard capture, TypeScript overload resolution, Kotlin and Swift inference report errors inside the combinator instead of at the offending step; add explicit type annotations at composition boundaries.

Lifting a chain into a monadic/Result context introduces bind/andThen semantics that differ from plain composition — associativity still holds but the algebra is different and casual reordering can change behaviour.

Wrong move: treat Ramda's compose and pipe as interchangeable -> Y fails because compose is right-to-left while pipe is left-to-right -> instead choose one direction and document it at each composition boundary.

Wrong move: use Redux compose for arbitrary asynchronous or failure-aware steps -> Y fails because enhancer composition does not model promise sequencing or error propagation -> instead use an async or Result-aware pipeline combinator.

Wrong move: make a long point-free chain when callback arguments or context matter -> Y fails because hidden argument order and receiver/context behavior become hard to debug -> instead name intermediate functions and pass explicit parameters.
